newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Hindalco profit seen lower in first half.
newsitem.headline: India's Hindalco profit seen lower in first half.

text.p: Depressed aluminium prices are likely to cause a fall in profit for the first half of the current fiscal year at India's largest private aluminium maker, Hindalco Industries, analysts said on Thursday.

Analysts forecast net profit would fall five or six percent to around 1.96-1.99 billion rupees ($54.8-55.6 million) in the first six months of fiscal 1996/97 (April-March), down from 2.08 billion in the first half of fiscal 1995/96.
Analysts forecast a marginal fall in net sales for the period. Sales had jumped almost 50 percent in the year-earlier period. Results are due on Monday.
Analysts largely blamed aluminium prices, which fell on the London Metal Exchange (LME) to a two-and-a-half year low in October.

"International aluminium prices fell sharply as LME inventories rose. Russian exports that were expected to fall did not come down and European and Japanese demand never revived," said an analyst at a European broking firm.

Analyst Rajesh Majumdar of securities firm Peregrine Capital said the average LME price of aluminium fell to $1,520 per tonne during April-September 1996, from an average of $1,800 in the same period a year earlier.
"Although prices have since improved marginally, the sentiment remains depressed," said Chetan Ahya, analyst at Caspian Securities.
The reduction in domestic aluminium prices was not as sharp, analysts said.

"Hindalco's clients include small producers like extrusion manufacturers for whom it is not viable to import, so to some extent the company is insulated from LME price fluctuations," said the analyst at the European broking firm.
Ahya at Caspian Securities said the company also suffered from power shortages from April to June due to a power grid failure.
Hindalco Chairman Kumar Mangalam Birla told shareholders at the firm's annual meeting in August that first-quarter gross sales were lower at 3.79 billion rupees.
But Birla said metal output would be higher in 1996/97 despite the first-quarter setback.
He added that the impact of current capital expenditures will begin to be felt from 1997/98.
Current projects include expansions of smelting and alumina capacities, enhancement of capacity at an existing captive power plant and modernisation of rolling mills.

"The second half should see a much better performance," said Peregrine's Majumdar. "Volumes will improve as production has come back to normal. The tax rate is expected to fall significantly due to ongoing capital expenditure."
